description_full: Haemonetics Corporation, a medical technology company, provides a suite of hospital technologies solutions. The company operates through Plasma, Blood Center, and Hospital segments. It provides automated plasma collection systems, donor management software, and supporting software solutions, such as NexSys PCS plasmapheresis equipment system and related disposables and solutions, as well as integrated information technology platforms for plasma customers to manage their donors, operations, and supply chain; and NexLynk DMS donor management system and Donor360 tools. The company also offers treatment in electrophysiology, critical care, neurocritical care, trauma, burn surgery, spine surgery, and cancer surgery; SavvyWire, a sensor-guided 3-in-1 guidewire for TAVR procedures; and OptoWire, a pressure guidewire that measures fractional flow reserve and diastolic pressure ratio, as well as fiber optic sensor solutions used in medical devices and other critical industrial applications. In addition, it provides hospital products comprising TEG 6s system, smallest cartridge-based viscoelastic analyzer that provides a comprehensive assessment of a patient's overall hemostasis; and TEG Manager software, which connects various TEG analyzers throughout the hospital, providing clinicians remote access to active and historical test results that inform treatment decisions. Further, the company offers Cell Saver Elite +, an autologous blood recovery system for cardiovascular, orthopedic, trauma, transplant, vascular, obstetrical, and gynecological surgeries;vascular closure products comprise VASCADE 5F, VASCADE 6/7F, VASCADE MVP XL, and VASCADE MVP, a technology platform which offers catheter-based delivery system and leverages the natural clot-inducing properties of collagen; and transfusion management solutions. It sells its products through direct sales force and independent distributors. The company was founded in 1971 and is headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Haemonetics Corporation is a mid-cap healthcare business with a $5.6B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 49%.

The business throws off $260M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 76%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $78.85 to $164 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.78).
It runs a 49% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 3.01x.
ROE of 12% is amplified by 3.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.6x net debt to EBITDA ($245.4M of cash against $1.2B of debt), with interest covered 8.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.3, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 230 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.5% over 3 years, 8.9% over 5 years and 3.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 98% of profits supports about 8.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 29.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 3% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 2%.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (2.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 26, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.3%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (3.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 3,009 employees, each generates about $443K of revenue, 1.2x the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 4.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $87K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
